rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, split-plot field experiment (DI vs SDI x 3 N rates, 5 reps) at KARE, California, 2013-2015. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3, in 2013 prime and subprime fruit weights were statistically different between SDI and DI (SDI higher, letters a/b); in 2015 subprime differed between systems; total yield never statistically different.
rows.notes: Supports the passage only for 2013 (prime and subprime higher under SDI); in 2015 the significant subprime difference was in favour of DI (18,246 vs 9,441 kg/ha). Single site, single crop, 1.4 ha field. Yield measured by one method only. Leaf N and soil nitrate were measured but the authors only assert ('can be explained in part') that N placement in the root zone drives the SDI advantage, so Q4 is no. Table 3 gives means with letter groupings only; 95% CIs mentioned in methods but not reported for yield, so Q9 no. No limitation of the yield result stated.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.7 and Table 8, residual weed biomass on 28 Aug 2013 was 81 g/m2 under SDI vs 569 g/m2 under DI, significantly lower (P=0.0001); Fig. 8 photo of 2012 weed differences. Q8: Section 3.7, authors state weed mass measurement was not conducted in other growing seasons, only observed qualitatively.
rows.notes: Weed biomass was quantified once (one date, one year, after herbicide burn-down). The infrared surface-temperature correlation (R=-0.636) is a consequence of weed cover rather than an independent measurement of weed pressure, and the other-year observations were visual only, so Q3 is no. Surface soil wetting (the presumed mechanism) was not measured. Table 8 reports means and P-values only.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment with weighing lysimeter and water meters. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 4, water productivity for total yield was consistently higher in SDI (60.4, 61.0, 59.7 kg/ha/mm) than DI (51.5, 53.4, 55.8); authors attribute this to higher average yields and lower applied water in SDI (843 vs 932 mm in 2015).
rows.notes: The lower water application to SDI was imposed by design (DI deliberately given ~10% more water for surface evaporation and weed use); soil evaporation was not measured, so Q4 no. WP values are means without dispersion; Table 5 letters only. The statement that additional study is required to test further SDI reductions is future work rather than a limitation of the WP result. Single site, one soil, one crop.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own split-plot field experiment. Q2: Section 3.4, Tables 3-4 and Conclusions, average yield was consistently higher in SDI than DI in all three years (e.g. 2013 prime 24,566 vs 22,850 kg/ha, significant), though total yield was not statistically different.
rows.notes: The higher SDI yield is a consistent but mostly non-significant difference (only 2013 prime/subprime significant). Mechanism (N placement near roots) is asserted, not demonstrated as a measured link to yield. Yield means reported without SD/SE/CI. Single site, crop and soil.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 4, water productivity (yield per mm applied) consistently higher under SDI than DI in 2013-2015 because of higher yields and less applied water in SDI.
rows.notes: Study reports water productivity (yield/applied water), used here as the WUE measure. The applied-water difference was set by design (10% extra to DI), not measured as a loss; no dispersion statistics for WP; single site.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.7 and Table 8, weed biomass 81 g/m2 under SDI vs 569 g/m2 under DI, significantly lower (P=0.0001). Q8: Section 3.7, weed mass was measured only in 2013, not in other seasons.
rows.notes: One quantitative sampling date in one year; other years only visual observation. IR surface temperature difference is a correlate, not an independent weed measurement. No SD or CI reported for weed biomass.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.4, Tables 3, 4 and 6, average yield, water productivity and (in 2013-2014) N productivity were higher under SDI than DI; Conclusions note a consistent non-statistical yield advantage for SDI.
rows.notes: Yield advantage of SDI was consistent but not statistically significant for total yield; NP was higher for SDI only in 2013 and 2014, not 2015. Means reported without dispersion; single site, soil and crop.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-site, three-year orchard experiment on Hanford sandy loam in California (1.4 ha field) comparing high-frequency surface and subsurface drip at three N rates; crop water use from one lysimeter tree irrigated with SDI. Significance reported as letter groupings or P-values; SE bars appear only for leaf/fruit N figures, not for yield, WP or weed data.
